quarterly_data.signal: CFO Eric Rivera laid out four reasons design releases (especially from foundry customers) were delayed in fiscal Q2: higher than normal fab utilization left fabs unable to accommodate additional design releases; chip OEMs prioritized revenue and profitability from existing products; the surge in memory prices and supply constraints delayed several new consumer electronic launches as OEMs worked to secure memory; and geopolitical developments including the US-Iran conflict. Visibility 'started becoming cloudy when the conflict with Iran and the U.S. started during the quarter.' Senior Executive for Asia Frank Lee said the post-Chinese New Year slowdown (seen at the end of February) was much longer than anticipated, the slowdown sits at the design houses at the very beginning of new design release, and the memory shortage hit mainly low-end consumer products in Taiwan and China; CEO George Macricostas said high-end consumer electronics launches have not been impacted by tight memory conditions.

Early recovery in order flow: Frank Lee said 'A lot of tape outs have happened since the beginning of May' after heavy tape-out delays in Q2, but Photronics remains very cautious; customers are still optimistic about the midterm outlook while near-term visibility remains limited. Rivera stressed visibility is limited with 'a typical backlog of only one to three weeks', that high-end mask sets carry significantly higher ASPs so a small number of orders can materially move revenue, and that most of the cost base is fixed with 'very little levers we can pull' if demand stays soft.
quarterly_data.figure: typical backlog of only one to three weeks

quarterly_data.signal: IC mix and AI demand: IC revenue represented 70% of total revenue and high-end represented 38% of IC. Macricostas said industry demand for leading-edge memory and logic chips for AI applications remains exceptionally strong and requires a significant number of high-end photomasks, a multi-year growth opportunity; the U.S. and Korea investments position Photronics for increased outsourcing from captive photomask producers, shifting mix toward more advanced geometries with higher ASPs. Rivera expects fiscal 2027 and 2028 revenue mix to shift by node toward high-end IC and geographically toward the U.S. and Korea. Taiwan and U.S. facilities are positioned for increasing advanced chip packaging opportunities.
quarterly_data.figure: IC 70% of total revenue; high-end 38% of IC

quarterly_data.signal: Node/site roadmap as of the Q2 call: in Korea the clean room is being prepared for key equipment to extend capabilities 'down to 8 nanometer and below', with installations expected to begin later in the fiscal year and initial revenue from the Korea expansion by the end of fiscal 2027. Boise, the high-end U.S. facility, 'is qualified to produce masks at the 7-nanometer node' for leading-edge AI chips, with teams working with customers on more advanced nodes; Rivera: 'Definitely we plan to go below those ranges.'
quarterly_data.figure: Korea down to 8 nanometer and below; Boise qualified at the 7-nanometer node; Korea initial revenue by the end of fiscal 2027

quarterly_data.signal: Allen, Texas: beginning production of qualification masks (qualifications started in Q3), targeting initial revenue late in the fiscal year with more meaningful contribution in 2027 and beyond; management does not expect the current environment to depress expected returns. Frank Lee said Allen is a technology upgrade, not just capacity: qualification is for technology Allen cannot do today, and Photronics plans to transfer some lower-end high-end and mainstream work from Boise to Allen to free Boise capacity for higher-ASP orders. Goal: 'We like to be the main photomask supplier in the United States.' Rivera expects the U.S. revenue percentage increase in 2027 to be larger than anywhere else.

Display (FPD) revenue of $62 million increased 13% year-over-year, one of the strongest quarters in the history of the display business, on more complex larger mask sizes and AMOLED differentiation; China demand shifted toward the high-end category and Korea re-accelerated ahead of fall consumer electronics launches. A recently installed FPD mask writer is entering production, aimed at G8.6 AMOLED, which carries higher ASP mask layers and is expected to be more widely adopted later in the calendar year.

Capex and cash as of the Q2 call: CapEx was $46 million (Korea 8 nanometer expansion, new Allen equipment, end-of-life tool upgrades, facility optimization); Photronics maintained fiscal 2026 CapEx guidance of $330 million, with elevated CapEx focused on strategic investments in the U.S. and Korea along with peak end-of-life tool upgrades, and is evaluating additional investment projects. Operating cash flow of $47 million was 22% of revenue; cash and short-term investments were flat at $638 million, including $477 million held within joint ventures in which Photronics holds a 50.1% ownership interest.
quarterly_data.figure: fiscal 2026 CapEx guidance of $330 million; operating cash flow $47 million (22% of revenue); cash $638 million incl. $477 million in joint ventures (50.1% ownership)
